extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method; practicing scientists interested in foundations of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and criteria for legitimate induction and the limits of tests of truth (e.g., inconceivability), including distinctions between genuine induction and mere enumeration or mathematical demonstration. Targets reasoning about when and how general propositions may be inferred from observed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability as a test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that an abortive effort to conceive the negation of a proposition shows the cognition is one we are compelled to accept (Spencer's test of inconceivableness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques this test: inconceivability often fails (e.g., sunrise/sunset) because people may habitually conceive phenomena differently from what they believe to be true; inability to conceive the negative may show only an inseparability in the mind that attempted the test, not an objective truth. The test is further limited because complex propositions are not legitimately tested in this way; only simple, immediately inspected propositions are candidates. Examples and counterexamples (sunrise, gravitation without medium, antipodes) are provided to show the test can yield false results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widespread belief is not conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a very general belief (e.g., in matter or other noumena) does not conclusively prove the truth of the thing believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such general belief is a psychological phenomenon that must be explained either by the truth of the belief or other causes (e.g., idola tribûs). Because the belief is a fact, opponents are called on to explain how so general and spontaneous a belief could have originated if the thing believed were not real; the success of such explanations will influence philosophical verdicts. This is an evidential standard: belief raises a burden of explanation but is not itself decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Postulate (Spencer): predicates invariably existing with their subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's reformulation: 'cognitions of which the predicates invariably exist along with their subjects'—if one cannot conceive the negation, this shows an invariable conjunction and thus the cognition must be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes two senses of 'invariable existence': (1) existence in actual nature/objective experience (if so, the proposition, once ascertained, compels acceptance), and (2) inseparability in our conceptive faculty (the ideas are inseparable in thought). Poincaré accepts both senses but warns that inseparability in thought does not prove inseparability in fact nor in other minds or future states. The Postulate's force depends on which sense is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: test applies only to immediately inspected simple propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconceivability test (and similar tests) is legitimately applicable only to simple propositions assented to on simple inspection without intervening media of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer himself limits his test to such elementary universal cognitions, represented in earliest and most unvarying experience. Complex propositions (those relying on chains of simple propositions) are not candidates for direct testing by inconceivability. Poincaré emphasizes that many historically false but once-inconceivable propositions were simple in character and so fall within the limitation, undermining the test's reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer appeal to experience over inconceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, test a proposition by appealing to experience itself rather than by relying on the inconceivability of its negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré argues that invoking experience (e.g., lifelong observation, unanimous reports from others) is a more direct and relevant test of truth than appealing to whether the negative is inconceivable; the inconceivability test only bears on familiarity, not sufficiency, of experience. He challenges Spencer's idea that one must mentally inspect every instance; rather, accumulated habitual observation and corroboration by others can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited mental tendencies do not guarantee truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if mental tendencies derived from ancestral experience become innate (a priori) in an individual, such inherited convictions may still be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré notes that if a conviction is innate because it was originally adaptive or derived from ancestors' experience, its present a priori character in the individual does not ensure its truth—original causes other than truth could have produced and transmitted the tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to conceive is not equivalent to demonstrative proof
rubrics_metrics.description: That we cannot conceive a contrary does not prove that a conclusion follows from premises; inability to conceive often only indicates compulsion to believe, not logical necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré contends that saying 'I cannot conceive that A is not C when I know A is B and B is C' amounts to being compelled to believe A is C, but may still allow mental representation of A not being C. Therefore, reasoning's evidence should not be reduced to mere inconceivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Contradiction as a generalization from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The Principle of Contradiction (an affirmative and its negative cannot both be true) is not merely verbal or identical but is a generalization founded on observed exclusion between belief and disbelief and on contrasts in phenomena (light/darkness, sound/silence, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré accepts it as an axiom grounded in observation of mental states and external contrasts, and recommends stating it simply: the same proposition cannot at the same time be false and true. He resists overstating it as a metaphysical fundamental antithesis pervading nature without this experiential grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Excluded Middle limited by meaningful predication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Principle of Excluded Middle (an assertion must be either true or false) is valid only when the predicate can intelligibly be attributed to the subject; otherwise a third possibility—'unmeaning'—exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré shows that for predicates that are not intelligibly applicable (e.g., 'Abracadabra is a second intention') the true/false dichotomy fails. Extending the principle to noumena (things-in-themselves) is therefore illegitimate because predicates like 'divisible' may be inapplicable or meaningless of things in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the operation of discovering and proving general propositions: inferring that what is true in particular observed cases will be true in all cases resembling them in assignable respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré emphasizes that this definition covers both establishing general laws and indirectly ascertaining individual facts; generals are collections of particulars, and an inference about an individual is equivalent in logic to a general inference over similar cases. The legitimacy of induction is the main question of logic of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of inductive principles across sciences and practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles and rules of induction are the same whether one infers general propositions or individual facts, and apply equally to scientific inquiry and practical reasoning (e.g., legal advocacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the choice or invention of which inductions to apply may require sagacity and subject knowledge, the validity of any induction when constructed depends on the same logical principles and tests of legitimacy across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between selection of inductions and their validity
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical inquiry the chief difficulty is selecting which known general propositions to apply; in contrast, the validity of the constructed argument depends on logical principles that can be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separates inventive/creative skill (choosing the right inductions to use) from the formal legitimacy of the inductions themselves; rules of logic judge the latter, not the former.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between real induction and mere enumeration (improper induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine induction infers a universal that goes beyond the particular instances observed; a mere summing up of known cases (e.g., 'all known planets') is not true induction but an abridged registration of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré gives examples: asserting 'all the planets shine by the sun's light' from observations of each known planet is not induction unless meant to assert 'all planets' (including unknown ones). A real induction's legitimacy depends on representativeness and the number/nature of instances, not completeness of enumeration. Beware the anti-pattern of treating an abridged notation as a substantive generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of instances depends on number and nature, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify a general proposition it is the number and the character (representativeness) of observed instances that matter, rather than having examined every individual of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré stresses that one may legitimately infer a general law without examining all known instances; conversely, an assertion limited to 'all known cases' is not a true generalization. Example: inferring 'all animals have a nervous system' may be induction if instances are sufficiently numerous and appropriately varied to ground the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstrations are not induction in the same sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Many mathematical 'generalizations' are not inductive in the empirical sense: proofs by diagram or parity of reasoning sum up demonstrative evidence rather than infer from particular instances to unknowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving a theorem for a particular geometric figure and then showing the same proof applies generally is not induction from observed cases but demonstration by general reasoning. Similarly, enumerating properties of all possible conic sections is not induction because no further instances exist beyond the demonstrated types. Mathematical 'calculation of series' sometimes looks inductive but relies on a priori considerations that could be exhibited as demonstration.
